stem: What does copyright protect?

options.content: An original work in its fixed form, such as program code, a document or a song
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: A bare idea that has not been written or recorded
options.rationale: Ideas are not protected until they are expressed in a work.

options.content: The name of a school
options.rationale: A name or logo may be a trademark.

options.content: Any information on a public web site, which anyone is free to copy, change and sell
options.rationale: Web content is still protected by copyright.

explanation: Copyright protects original works, not bare ideas.

stem: Why is copyright legislation needed for software?

options.content: Copies are perfect and cheap to make, so without a law creators could not earn a reward for their work
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Software cannot be copied at all
options.rationale: Software is easy to copy, which is why the law is needed.

options.content: Only large companies write software, so only they need to be protected by the law
options.rationale: Individuals and small teams also create software.

options.content: Copyright makes software run faster
options.rationale: Copyright does not affect performance.

explanation: The law lets creators control copying and earn a reward.

stem: Which type of licence lets a user try a program for a limited time and pay to keep using it?

options.content: Site licence
options.rationale: A site licence covers many computers at one site for a fixed fee.

options.content: Open source
options.rationale: Open-source software makes its source code available.

options.content: Freeware
options.rationale: Freeware has no payment at all.

options.content: Shareware
options.rationale: Correct.

stem: A school has 40 computers and wants the same office software on all of them for a single fee. Which licence is suitable?

options.content: A single-user licence for each computer, bought separately
options.rationale: This would cost more than a fixed fee for many computers.

options.content: A trial version of shareware
options.rationale: A trial version stops working or is limited.

options.content: A licence that allows one copy only
options.rationale: One copy would not cover 40 computers.

options.content: A site licence
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A site licence covers any number of computers at one site.

stem: A rural clinic has no money for software and needs to be able to adapt a program for its own forms. Which kind of software is the best choice?

options.content: Commercial software with a restrictive licence
options.rationale: It costs money and cannot be changed.

options.content: A pirated copy of commercial software
options.rationale: Using a pirated copy is illegal.

options.content: Open-source software
options.rationale: Correct: it has no fee and the source code can be changed.

options.content: Freeware whose licence does not allow changes
options.rationale: It cannot be adapted.

explanation: Open source gives legal use and the freedom to adapt.
hints: Which licence allows both low cost and changes?

stem: How does similarity-checking software help to detect plagiarism?

options.content: It deletes any text that has been copied
options.rationale: It only reports matches.

options.content: It compares a document with a store of other documents and reports the text that matches
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It writes the missing references for the author and corrects the copied text
options.rationale: It does not write references.

options.content: It proves that the author is guilty
options.rationale: The report is a guide; a person must judge.

explanation: The checker reports matches; a person decides if they are plagiarism.
hints: Does the software decide, or does it report?

stem: A student includes a paragraph from a web site in a report, in quotation marks, with the source named. Which statement is correct?

options.content: It is plagiarism because the paragraph came from the internet, whatever the source is
options.rationale: Acknowledged quotation is acceptable.

options.content: It is piracy of software
options.rationale: Piracy concerns software licences, not quotations.

options.content: It is not plagiarism because the source is acknowledged, although it may still count in a similarity report
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It is fine to copy a whole chapter in the same way
options.rationale: Only a short extract may be quoted for study.

explanation: Acknowledged quotations are allowed; the checker may still show them as matches.
hints: What makes plagiarism different from quotation?

stem: Which is the strongest reason to buy licensed software rather than use a pirated copy?

options.content: Pirated software always runs slower
options.rationale: Speed is not the main difference.

options.content: The licensed copy is legal, gets updates and support, and carries less risk of hidden malware
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Licensed software never needs updating
options.rationale: All software needs updates.

options.content: A licence guarantees that the program has no mistakes and will never need updates
options.rationale: No licence can guarantee that.

explanation: Legal use, updates and lower risk are the main advantages.
hints: Think about the law, support and security.

stem: What does a patent protect?

options.content: The name and logo of a firm, shown on its goods
options.rationale: That is a trademark.

options.content: A new invention, for a limited time
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The text of a novel
options.rationale: That is protected by copyright.

options.content: A password
options.rationale: A patent does not protect passwords.

explanation: A patent protects how an invention works.
hints: Is it an invention, a name or a written work?

stem: In free software as defined by the Free Software Foundation, "free" refers to the freedom to use, study, change and share the program, not to its price.
explanation: True. Free software is about freedom; it may or may not be sold.

stem: Match each type of software to its description.

right.content: No payment needed, but the source code is usually not provided
The source code is available to use, study, change and share
One fee for use on any number of computers at one site
Paid for, with copying and sharing restricted by the licence
Free to try for a limited time, then payment is needed

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Using software without the licence required is called software {{blank:a}}. Presenting another person's work as your own is called {{blank:b}}. The legal right of a creator to control copying of an original work is called {{blank:c}}.

hints: One is about software, one about someone's work.

stem: Name the form of intellectual property that protects a company's name or logo.
A program costs US\$30 for each computer. Calculate the cost of individual licences for 20 computers.
hints: Multiply the number of computers by the price of one licence.

stem: A site licence costs US\$420. Individual licences cost US\$30 each. Calculate the number of computers at which the two options cost the same.
hints: The break-even number is the site fee divided by the price of one licence.

stem: A similarity checker finds that 90 words of a 600-word essay match other sources. Calculate the percentage of the essay that matches.
Explain why copyright legislation is needed. [3]

points.description: Digital work can be copied perfectly, cheaply and quickly, so without a law creators could lose their income
The law makes unauthorised copying and selling an offence, which deters people
It encourages creators to produce new software and other work because they can be rewarded

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Digital work can be copied perfectly, cheaply and quickly, so creators could lose their income. The law makes unauthorised copying an offence, which deters people, and it encourages new work because creators can be rewarded.

hints: Think about creators, copying and rewards.

stem: A software company in Harare writes an accounting program and wants to earn money from every business that uses it. State the type of licence it should use and justify your choice. [4]

points.description: A commercial (proprietary) licence
Customers pay a fee, so the company earns money from every user
The source code is not provided, so others cannot copy or sell the program
The licence restricts copying and sharing, and can include support and updates for paying customers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A commercial licence. Customers must pay a fee, so the company earns from every user. The source code is not provided and copying is restricted, so others cannot copy or sell the program, and support and updates can be offered to paying customers.

hints: Name the licence and give two reasons that fit the scenario.

stem: Compare open-source software with commercial software. [4]

points.description: Open-source software has its source code available; commercial software does not provide it
Open-source users may change and share the software; commercial users are restricted by the licence
Open-source software is often free of cost, while commercial software must be paid for
Commercial software normally includes support and updates from the company, which open-source software may lack

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Open-source software has its source code available and users may change and share it; commercial software does not provide source code and restricts copying. Open-source software is often free of cost, while commercial software must be paid for but usually includes support and updates.

explanation: Source code, freedom, cost and support.
hints: Compare cost, source code and freedom to share.

stem: Describe how software piracy and plagiarism can each be detected. [4]

points.description: Piracy: product activation or licence keys checked online show that a copy is not licensed
Piracy: audits compare the software installed with the licences held
Plagiarism: similarity-checking software compares the work with a store of documents and reports matching text
A person then examines the matches to decide if the text is copied, because the percentage is only a guide

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Piracy is detected by activation and licence keys checked online and by audits comparing installed software with licences held. Plagiarism is detected by similarity-checking software that reports matching text, which a person then examines because the percentage is only a guide.

hints: Describe how each is found, then what is done.

stem:
A school in Masvingo is choosing how to license a program. Individual licences cost US\$30 each. A site licence costs US\$420 for any number of computers.

| Computers | Individual licences (US\$) | Site licence (US\$) | Cheaper |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 8 | 240 | 420 | Individual |
| 14 | 420 | 420 | Same |
| 20 | 600 | 420 | Site |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many computers cost the same under both options?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The school has 20 computers. State which option is cheaper (individual or site).
parts.explanation: 20 × 30 = US$600 for individual licences, which is more than US$420.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate how much the school saves by buying a site licence for 20 computers instead of individual licences.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Give two reasons other than cost why the school might choose open-source software instead.

points.description: The source code can be changed to fit the school's needs
There is no risk of breaking licence conditions when the software is copied to more computers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The source code can be changed to fit the school's needs, and the software can be copied to more computers without breaking licence conditions.

explanation: For 8 computers individual licences are cheaper, at 14 they cost the same and at 20 the site licence is cheaper.
hints: Individual cost = number × price; compare with the site fee.

stem: A teacher at a school in Mutare receives a project report of 1250 words. A similarity checker reports that 300 words match other sources. The teacher finds that 50 of these words are a quotation with the source acknowledged.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of the report that the checker reports as matching.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage that remains after the acknowledged quotation is excluded.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the teacher should not decide from the percentage alone that the learner has plagiarised.

points.description: The matches may be common phrases, references or acknowledged quotations, which are not plagiarism
A person must read the matched passages and judge whether the work was passed off as the learner's own

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The matches may be common phrases, references or quotations that are acknowledged, which are not plagiarism, so a person must read the passages and judge.

stem: Three owners want to protect their work. A: an engineer in Bulawayo has invented a new type of water-level sensor. B: a firm in Harare has a logo and a name for its internet service. C: a student in Gweru has written a program.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the form of protection most suitable for A.
parts.explanation: A patent protects a new invention.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the form of protection most suitable for B.
parts.explanation: A trademark protects names and logos.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the form of protection that automatically applies to the program in C.
parts.explanation: Copyright arises automatically when a work is created.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the owner of B is protected by the law against a rival firm that copies the logo.

points.description: The trademark gives the owner the exclusive right to use the logo for its services
The owner can take legal action against the rival firm
Customers are protected because they are not misled into thinking the rival's services come from firm B

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The trademark gives the owner the exclusive right to use the logo for its services, so the owner can take legal action against the rival, and customers are protected from being misled.

explanation: A is a patent, B is a trademark and C is copyright.
hints: Patents protect inventions; trademarks protect names and logos.
